setup.zh: 娘把最后一点白面烙成两张饼，厚的给你；爹拿麻布缠紧了膝盖。娘说：打得过就打，打不过就跑。
setup.en: Mother bakes the last of the white flour into two flatbreads, the thick one for you; Father binds his knee tight. Mother says: fight if you can win; if not, run.

recap.zh: 娘把最后一点白面烙成饼塞给你：「打不过就跑——跑不丢人。」
recap.en: Mother gave you bread from the last of the flour: "If you can't win, run — there's no shame in running."

zh: 灶间亮了灯。最后一点白面，烙成两张饼。
en: A lamp in the kitchen. The last of the flour, baked into two flatbreads.
"When something happens, think first; move when you've thought it through."

story.zh:
他关上窗，一回身，灶间的灯已经亮了，他娘蹲在灶前烙饼，烙的竟是白面的。家里那只装白面的小布袋，小满知道，已经瘪了一个月了。

他娘把最后一点面全抖了出来，抖了三遍，连布袋缝里的面粉都拍了个干净，烙成了两张饼，一张厚，一张薄。
story.en:
He shut the window, turned round, and the lamp in the kitchen was already lit. His mother was crouched at the stove making flatbread — and white-flour flatbread at that. The little cloth bag that held the family's white flour, Xiaoman knew, had been flat for a month.

His mother had shaken out every last bit of flour, shaken it three times, even patted the seams of the bag clean, and made two flatbreads, one thick, one thin.

exits.means: sets off with father into the mountain, moves on

refuse.zh: 鏊子上的饼还没烙好——火，归你看着。
refuse.en: The bread on the griddle isn't done yet — the fire is yours to mind.

story_after.zh:
他娘没回头，问道：「他爹，你真要去黑松岭？」他爹道：「前山叫马家篦空了，不去不行。」他娘道：「你那腿——」他爹道：「我这腿是不行了。」顿了一顿，又道：「还有孩子的腿。」

她把那张厚的饼铲了出来，塞进小满怀里；薄的那张，给了他爹；她自己一张也没有。

她蹲下来，看着小满的眼睛：「你爹老实。一辈子不会算计人，也不会防着人。你不一样。你随我。」又道：「山里的东西，比马三还狠。遇事要先想，想好了再动。想明白了，打得过就打，打不过就跑。跑，不丢人。」

他娘道：「还有一件事。昨天那一下，娘看见了。」小满抬起头来。他娘道：「你没还手。对的。」又道：「你回的那句嘴——也对。」她伸手把他额前的头发拢了拢，道：「可也别忘了。」

他娘站在门口——门口其实没有门，门还在阿禾家的菜地里——看着一大一小两个背影，走进天边那一线灰白里去。她没有喊，也没有挥手，就那么一直站着，直站到小满回头也看不见她了。
story_after.en:
His mother didn't turn round. "Husband, are you really going to Black Pine Ridge?" His father said, "The Mas have combed the near hills bare. There's nothing for it." His mother said, "Your leg—" His father said, "My leg's no good any more." He paused, then said, "There's the boy's legs as well."

She lifted out the thick flatbread and tucked it inside Xiaoman's jacket. The thin one she gave to his father. She had none herself.

She crouched down and looked Xiaoman in the eye: "Your father's an honest man. All his life he's never schemed against anyone, and never guarded against anyone either. You're different. You take after me." "Things in the mountains are fiercer than Ma San. When something happens, think first, and move once you've thought it through. Once you've worked it out: if you can beat it, fight; if you can't, run. There's no shame in running."

His mother said, "One more thing. Yesterday — I saw it." Xiaoman looked up. His mother said, "You didn't hit back. That was right." "And what you said back to him — that was right too." She brushed the hair back from his forehead. "But don't forget it, either."

His mother stood in the doorway — there wasn't actually a door in the doorway; the door was still in Ahe's vegetable plot — and watched the two backs, one big, one small, walk off into the thin grey line at the edge of the sky. She didn't call out, and she didn't wave. She just stood there, and stood there, until Xiaoman looked back and couldn't see her any more.

story_after_full.zh:
他爹坐在炕沿上，拿一块旧麻布一圈一圈地缠他的左膝，缠完了站起身来，试着走了两步，脸上的肉抽了一下，又若无其事地坐了回去，冲小满咧嘴一笑，道：「没事。老毛病。它今天话有点多。」

他娘没回头，问道：「他爹，你真要去黑松岭？」他爹道：「前山叫马家篦空了，不去不行。」他娘道：「你那腿——」他爹道：「我这腿是不行了。」顿了一顿，又道：「还有孩子的腿。」

他娘手里的铲子停了一下。跟着她把那张厚的饼铲了出来，拿一块干净的布包好，走过来塞进小满怀里；薄的那张，给了他爹；她自己一张也没有。

她蹲下来，看着小满的眼睛，声音压得极低，低得只有他们两个听得见：「你爹老实。一辈子不会算计人，也不会防着人。你不一样。你随我。」

说着伸手掐掉了他衣襟上的一根线头，又道：「山里的东西，比马三还狠。遇事要先想，想好了再动。想明白了，打得过就打，打不过就跑。跑，不丢人。」

小满道：「嗯，娘，我记住了。」他娘道：「还有一件事。昨天那一下，娘看见了。」小满抬起头来。他娘道：「你没还手。对的。」她的嘴角极轻极轻地动了一下，又道：「你回的那句嘴——也对。」她伸手把他额前的头发拢了拢，道：「可也别忘了。」

他爹在身后咳了两声，背起了那张弓。他娘站在门口——门口其实没有门，门还在阿禾家的菜地里——看着一大一小两个背影，走进天边那一线灰白里去。她没有喊，也没有挥手，就那么一直站着，直站到小满回头也看不见她了。
story_after_full.en:
His father sat on the edge of the bed wrapping his left knee round and round with a strip of old sacking. When he was done he stood up and tried a couple of steps. The muscles in his face twitched once, and then he sat back down as if nothing had happened, and grinned at Xiaoman. "It's fine. Old trouble. It's a bit talkative today."

His mother didn't turn round. "Husband, are you really going to Black Pine Ridge?" His father said, "The Mas have combed the near hills bare. There's nothing for it." His mother said, "Your leg—" His father said, "My leg's no good any more." He paused, then said, "There's the boy's legs as well."

The spatula in his mother's hand stopped for a moment. Then she lifted out the thick flatbread, wrapped it in a clean cloth, came over and tucked it inside Xiaoman's jacket. The thin one she gave to his father. She had none herself.

She crouched down and looked Xiaoman in the eye, her voice pressed so low only the two of them could hear: "Your father's an honest man. All his life he's never schemed against anyone, and never guarded against anyone either. You're different. You take after me."

She reached out and pinched off a loose thread on his collar. "Things in the mountains are fiercer than Ma San. When something happens, think first, and move once you've thought it through. Once you've worked it out: if you can beat it, fight; if you can't, run. There's no shame in running."

Xiaoman said, "Yes, Ma. I'll remember." His mother said, "One more thing. Yesterday — I saw it." Xiaoman looked up. His mother said, "You didn't hit back. That was right." The corner of her mouth moved, very, very slightly. "And what you said back to him — that was right too." She brushed the hair back from his forehead. "But don't forget it, either."

Behind them his father coughed twice and shouldered the bow. His mother stood in the doorway — there wasn't actually a door in the doorway; the door was still in Ahe's vegetable plot — and watched the two backs, one big, one small, walk off into the thin grey line at the edge of the sky. She didn't call out, and she didn't wave. She just stood there, and stood there, until Xiaoman looked back and couldn't see her any more.
